evidence.claim: AWS DR guidance describes four strategies in increasing cost and complexity: backup and restore (lowest cost, longest RTO), pilot light (RTO/RPO in tens of minutes), warm standby (RTO/RPO in minutes) and multi-site active/active (RPO near zero, RTO potentially zero). Active/active is the most complex and should only be selected when business requirements necessitate it. In a worked example, AWS says pilot light or warm standby satisfies both the RTO and the cost criteria.

evidence.claim: Multi-leader active-active writes make conflicts unavoidable. Common guidance: keep financial ledger writes strongly consistent, route each entity's writes to a home region, or default to active-passive.

evidence.claim: Google Cloud Spanner uses synchronous Paxos-based replication: voting replicas vote on every write, and a write commits once a majority agrees. In multi-region configurations every write needs a quorum across replicas in more than one region, so writes have higher latency than in single-region instances. Read-only replicas do not vote and do not add write latency. Google says RPO and RTO are 0 for a multi-region configuration when writes come from near the default leader region.
evidence.applicability: D3/G6: near-zero-RPO cross-region standby is achievable with synchronous quorum replication, at the cost of cross-region round-trip latency on every write. It typically needs three or more locations for quorum rather than two (consistent with E15's split-brain concern).
evidence.limitations: Snippets only. All sources are Google (different domains but the same vendor, so not fully independent). No specific millisecond figures retrieved from an official source. The 100-200 ms figure in E15 is from low-authority blogs, and actual cost depends on region-pair distance. Spanner-specific; adopting it would mean a database migration.

verification.method: Search snippets from Google docs and blog

evidence.claim: An engineering post on cross-region single-leader replication (PostgreSQL) notes that synchronous cross-region acknowledgment puts the wide-area network directly into the commit path. A synchronous setting without selected standbys does not create cross-region durability, and acknowledgment alone does not guarantee zero loss of acknowledged writes if the primary site disappears before the standby catches up (e.g. remote_write vs applied semantics).

source.title: How to Design Cross-Region Single-Leader Replication Without Surprise Latency

evidence.applicability: D3/G6: zero-RPO standby on a conventional RDBMS is possible with synchronous or semi-synchronous replication, but every commit then pays at least one cross-region round trip, and the guarantee depends on configuration details. This is a cheaper middle option than multi-writer active-active for the ledger.
evidence.limitations: Single third-party snippet. No latency numbers retrieved. MySQL semi-synchronous replication specifics were not found (see E32).

evidence.claim: No authoritative figures were found for (a) MySQL semi-synchronous cross-region commit latency, (b) measured (as opposed to design-target) end-to-end warm standby failover times including human decision time, or (c) a vendor-published end-to-end regional failover time.

evidence.claim: Taken together, E21-E24 show that the largest recent cloud outages often spread through shared global layers (control-plane endpoints anchored in one region, globally replicated policy/config, global edge/DNS) rather than staying inside one region. A same-provider second region does not remove these dependencies. Config-push failures at provider scale are the same failure class as the company's own dominant incident cause (bad config/deploy pushes, E3).
evidence.applicability: D1/C1/C6: strengthens the case that region-scoped redundancy addresses only part of provider-outage risk, and that change-safety controls (staged, validated, fail-open config rollout) target both the company's and the providers' dominant failure mode.
evidence.limitations: Synthesis across snippet-level sources. Three or four events are anecdotes, not a base rate. No documented multi-region outage caused by certificate issuance was retrieved in this run (not searched due to budget).
